claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about axoneme structure.

claims.claim: Cilia play essential roles in cell motility, generate the movement of fluids over multiciliated surfaces, and sense extracellular signals.
claims.source: Cilia play essential roles in cell motility, generate the movement of fluids over multiciliated surfaces, and sense extracellular signals (Satir et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The IFT machinery transports axonemal precursors and sensory proteins bidirectionally between the cell body and the ciliary tip.
claims.source: To assemble and maintain functional cilia, the IFT machinery (Kozminski et al., 1993) transports axonemal precursors and sensory proteins bidirectionally between the cell body and the ciliary tip.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Defects in IFT are linked to a wide range of human diseases including Bardet-Biedl syndrome, retinal degeneration, and polycystic kidney disease.
claims.source: Defects in IFT are linked to a wide range of human diseases including Bardet-Biedl syndrome, retinal degeneration, and polycystic kidney disease (Brown and Witman, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Intraflagellar cargoes interact with multiprotein complexes known as IFT particles that are organized into larger IFT trains as they enter the flagellum.
claims.source: Intraflagellar cargoes interact with multiprotein complexes known as IFT particles that are organized into larger IFT trains as they enter the flagellum (Cole et al., 1998; Lechtreck et al., 2017; Pigino et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: In most species, the IFT trains are transported anterogradely from the base to the tip of a flagellum by heterotrimeric kinesin-II.
claims.source: In most species, the IFT trains are transported anterogradely from the base to the tip of a flagellum by heterotrimeric kinesin-II (Kozminski et al., 1995), but some species also use a second homodimeric kinesin to build more specialized sensory cilia (Snow et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Some species use a second homodimeric kinesin to build more specialized sensory cilia.
claims.source: In most species, the IFT trains are transported anterogradely from the base to the tip of a flagellum by heterotrimeric kinesin-II (Kozminski et al., 1995), but some species also use a second homodimeric kinesin to build more specialized sensory cilia (Snow et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Once the trains reach the tip, they are reorganized and transported retrogradely to the ciliary base by dynein-1b.
claims.source: Once the trains reach the tip, they are reorganized and transported retrogradely to the ciliary base by dynein-1b (Pazour et al., 1999; Porter et al., 1999; Signor et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Along the length of a cilium, the activities of kinesin and dynein motors are reciprocally coordinated, such that only one type of a motor is active at a time.
claims.source: Along the length of a cilium, the activities of kinesin and dynein motors are reciprocally coordinated, such that only one type of a motor is active at a time (Shih et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Trains move between the tip and base of the cilium without significant pauses or back-and-forth motion.
claims.source: As a result, trains move between the tip and base of the cilium without significant pauses or back-and-forth motion (Dentler, 2005; Engel et al., 2009) and switch directions at the turnaround zones (Ishikawa and Marshall, 2011; Laib et al., 2009; Shih et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Trains switch directions at the turnaround zones.
claims.source: As a result, trains move between the tip and base of the cilium without significant pauses or back-and-forth motion (Dentler, 2005; Engel et al., 2009) and switch directions at the turnaround zones (Ishikawa and Marshall, 2011; Laib et al., 2009; Shih et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Dynein-1b requires kinesin-II activity to reach the ciliary tip.
claims.source: Dynein-1b requires kinesin-II activity to reach the ciliary tip, suggesting that it travels on anterograde trains (Iomini et al., 2001; Pedersen et al., 2006; Rompolas et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Retrograde traces of kinesin-II have not been frequently observed in Chlamydomonas.
claims.source: Retrograde traces of kinesin-II have not been frequently observed in Chlamydomonas, and it remains unclear how kinesin-II returns to the basal body (Engel et al., 2009; Wingfield et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Anterograde and retrograde IFT trains have different sizes and depart at different frequencies.
claims.source: Because anterograde and retrograde IFT trains have different sizes and depart at different frequencies (Dentler, 2005; Iomini et al., 2001), IFT trains must be remodeled at the distal tip and the flagellar base.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: IFT trains must be remodeled at the distal tip and the flagellar base.
claims.source: Because anterograde and retrograde IFT trains have different sizes and depart at different frequencies (Dentler, 2005; Iomini et al., 2001), IFT trains must be remodeled at the distal tip and the flagellar base.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on cited observations about train size and frequency differences.

claims.claim: The mechanism underlying the remodeling of IFT complexes at the ciliary tip and base cannot be directly observed by conventional microscopy methods because multiple trains coexist in these turnaround zones.
claims.source: The mechanism underlying the remodeling of IFT complexes at the ciliary tip and base cannot be directly observed by conventional microscopy methods because multiple trains coexist in these turnaround zones (Buisson et al., 2013; Iomini et al., 2001; Wren et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations supported by citations.

claims.claim: The velocity of IFT27-GFP was 2.1 ± 0.4 µm s−1 in the anterograde direction.
claims.source: The velocity of IFT27-GFP was 2.1 ± 0.4 µm s−1 in the anterograde direction and 3.0 ± 0.7 µm s−1 in the retrograde direction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, mean ± s.d., N = 80 trains in each direction).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiments reported in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The velocity of IFT27-GFP was 3.0 ± 0.7 µm s−1 in the retrograde direction.
claims.source: The velocity of IFT27-GFP was 2.1 ± 0.4 µm s−1 in the anterograde direction and 3.0 ± 0.7 µm s−1 in the retrograde direction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, mean ± s.d., N = 80 trains in each direction).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiments reported in the manuscript.

claims.claim: On average, 2.4 retrograde trains were detected departing from the tip after the arrival of a single fluorescent anterograde train.
claims.source: On average, 2.4 retrograde trains were detected departing from the tip after the arrival of a single fluorescent anterograde train (Figure 1f, N = 97), consistent with higher frequencies of retrograde IFT trains than anterograde IFT trains (Dentler, 2005; Iomini et al., 2001; Qin et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments reported in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The number of retrograde trains per fluorescent anterograde train in PhotoGate assays (2.4) was significantly higher than the ratio of retrograde to anterograde train frequencies (1.15).
claims.source: However, the number of retrograde trains per fluorescent anterograde train in PhotoGate assays (2.4, Figure 1c) was significantly higher (Welch's t-test, p=10−20) than the ratio of retrograde to anterograde train frequencies (1.15, Figure 1a) (Dentler, 2005; Iomini et al., 2001; Reck et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental measurements with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: IFT complexes from different anterograde trains recombine with each other to form retrograde trains at the tip.
claims.source: These observations suggested that IFT complexes from different anterograde trains recombine with each other to form retrograde trains at the tip.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PhotoGate experiments showing sub-proportional increase in retrograde trains.

claims.claim: The fluorescent complexes in the anterograde trains disassemble and mix with a pool of 'dark' complexes from the other photobleached trains at the tip before they reorganize into retrograde trains.
claims.source: Because the increase was sub-proportional with the number of anterograde trains, we concluded that the fluorescent complexes in the anterograde trains disassemble and mix with a pool of 'dark' complexes from the other photobleached trains at the tip before they reorganize into retrograde trains (Figure 1f).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the sub-proportional increase in retrograde trains observed in the experiments.

claims.claim: The tip resting time of the first retrograde train was 3.1 ± 0.3 s.
claims.source: When only a single fluorescent anterograde IFT27-GFP train was left unbleached near the base of the flagellum, the tip resting time of the first retrograde train was 3.1 ± 0.3 s (mean ± s.e.m., N = 97, Figure 2b), comparable to that of IFT cargos (Craft et al., 2015; Reck et al., 2016; Wren et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments.

claims.claim: The tip resting time histogram of first retrograde trains fit well to a Gamma distribution with a shape parameter of 3 and a rate constant of ~1 s−1.
claims.source: However, the tip resting time histogram of first retrograde trains fit well to a Gamma distribution with a shape parameter of 3 and a rate constant of ~1 s−1, indicating that tip turnaround of IFT trains occurs rapidly through a multistep process (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Tip turnaround of IFT trains occurs rapidly through a multistep process.
claims.source: However, the tip resting time histogram of first retrograde trains fit well to a Gamma distribution with a shape parameter of 3 and a rate constant of ~1 s−1, indicating that tip turnaround of IFT trains occurs rapidly through a multistep process (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Gamma distribution fit to the data.

claims.claim: The average time between successive retrograde trains (Δt) is 1.7 s.
claims.source: We also observed that the tip resting time of first, second, third, and fourth fluorescent retrograde trains increases linearly (Figure 2c). Because the average time between successive retrograde trains (Δt = 1.7 s) is the same, we concluded that the tip departure is a purely stochastic process.
claims.evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The tip departure is a purely stochastic process.
claims.source: We also observed that the tip resting time of first, second, third, and fourth fluorescent retrograde trains increases linearly (Figure 2c). Because the average time between successive retrograde trains (Δt = 1.7 s) is the same, we concluded that the tip departure is a purely stochastic process.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the linear increase in tip resting times with constant intervals.

claims.claim: The linear fit to the tip resting times has a y-intercept of 1.3 s.
claims.source: The linear fit to the tip resting times has a y-intercept of 1.3 s (Figure 2c), revealing that the departure of the first train takes longer than Δt.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the linear fit analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: The complexes dwell at the tip through another rate limiting process before they can depart from the tip.
claims.source: The linear fit to the tip resting times has a y-intercept of 1.3 s (Figure 2c), revealing that the departure of the first train takes longer than Δt. Therefore, the complexes dwell at the tip through another rate limiting process before they can depart from the tip.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the y-intercept being longer than the interval between successive trains.

claims.claim: When extracellular calcium in media (0.34 mM) was chelated using 0.5 mM EGTA, the tip departure time increased to 2.8 s.
claims.source: When extracellular calcium in media (0.34 mM) was chelated using 0.5 mM EGTA, the tip departure time increased to 2.8 s (Welch's t-test, p=0.01), whereas tip remodeling time (1.4 s) remained unaltered (Figure 2d,e).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the EGTA treatment experiments.

claims.claim: Tip remodeling time (1.4 s) remained unaltered when extracellular calcium was chelated using 0.5 mM EGTA.
claims.source: When extracellular calcium in media (0.34 mM) was chelated using 0.5 mM EGTA, the tip departure time increased to 2.8 s (Welch's t-test, p=0.01), whereas tip remodeling time (1.4 s) remained unaltered (Figure 2d,e).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the EGTA treatment experiments.

claims.claim: Calcium has minimal effect on the breakdown of anterograde trains, but may have a regulatory role in the assembly or departure of retrograde trains.
claims.source: Therefore, calcium has minimal effect on the breakdown of anterograde trains, but may have a regulatory role in the assembly or departure of retrograde trains.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of EGTA on tip remodeling vs. departure times.

claims.claim: Addition of 0.1 mM ciliobrevin D to media results in 50% reduction in the frequency of retrograde and anterograde trains.
claims.source: Addition of 0.1 mM ciliobrevin D to media results in 50% reduction in the frequency of retrograde and anterograde trains, and 50% and 28% reduction in retrograde and anterograde train velocities, respectively (Shih et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claims.claim: The tip resting time of IFT27 increased over two-fold with ciliobrevin D treatment.
claims.source: In this case, the tip resting time of IFT27 increased over two-fold (Figure 2e, p<10−4), suggesting that rapid turnover of IFT trains depends on dynein activity.
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the ciliobrevin D treatment experiments.

claims.claim: Rapid turnover of IFT trains depends on dynein activity.
claims.source: In this case, the tip resting time of IFT27 increased over two-fold (Figure 2e, p<10−4), suggesting that rapid turnover of IFT trains depends on dynein activity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the effect of the dynein inhibitor ciliobrevin D on tip resting time.

claims.claim: D1bLIC moved continuously in the anterograde and retrograde directions at velocities similar to that of the IFT trains.
claims.source: In the d1blic::D1bLIC-GFP strain, D1bLIC moved continuously in the anterograde and retrograde directions at velocities similar to that of the IFT trains (Reck et al., 2016) (Figure 3a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claims.claim: KAP moved primarily in the anterograde direction to the flagellar tip at a similar speed to anterograde IFT27.
claims.source: In the fla3::KAP-GFP strain, KAP moved primarily in the anterograde direction to the flagellar tip at a similar speed to anterograde IFT27 (Figure 3b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Retrograde traces of KAP were not frequently observed.
claims.source: Unlike D1bLIC, retrograde traces of KAP were not frequently observed (Engel et al., 2009; Wingfield et al., 2017), suggesting that kinesin-II dissociates from IFT trains at the tip (Engel et al., 2009; Engel et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the imaging experiments supported by citations.

claims.claim: After arrival of a single anterograde D1bLIC-GFP train at the tip, on average 2.5 retrograde D1bLIC trains were detected.
claims.source: After arrival of a single anterograde D1bLIC-GFP train at the tip, we detected on average 2.5 retrograde D1bLIC trains.
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments.

claims.claim: The average tip resting time until the departure of the first retrograde D1bLIC train was 1.8 ± 0.2 s.
claims.source: The average tip resting time until the departure of the first retrograde train was 1.8 ± 0.2 s (mean ± s.e.m., N = 60, Figure 3d), with additional ~1.1 ± 0.1 s between subsequent departure events (Figure 3e).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments.

claims.claim: Single KAP-GFP trains moved anterogradely to the tip and rested at the tip for 2.2 ± 0.2 s.
claims.source: PhotoGate imaging of KAP-GFP cells showed that single KAP-GFP trains moved anterogradely to the tip and rested at the tip for 2.2 ± 0.2 s (N = 95).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the PhotoGate experiments.

claims.claim: Individual KAP-GFP particles moved away from the tip by rapid saltatory motion.
claims.source: Unlike D1bLIC, individual KAP-GFP particles moved away from the tip by rapid saltatory motion (Figure 3f,g, Figure 1—figure supplement 2c, Video 6).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the PhotoGate experiments.

claims.claim: KAP undergoes one-dimensional diffusion at 1.68 ± 0.04 µm2 s−1 within the flagellum after it departs from the tip.
claims.source: Mean square displacement (MSD) analysis showed that KAP undergoes one-dimensional diffusion at 1.68 ± 0.04 µm2 s−1 (mean ± s.e.m., N = 27 traces) within the flagellum after it departs from the tip (Figure 3h), consistent with the values measured for tubulin and EB1 that undergo diffusion within the ciliary space (Craft et al., 2015; Harris et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from MSD analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: The tip resting time of KAP remained nearly constant at different steady-state flagellar lengths.
claims.source: The tip resting time of KAP remained nearly constant at different steady-state flagellar lengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and was shorter than that of IFT27, indicating that departure of kinesin from the tip is independent of flagellar length and departure of retrograde trains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments at different flagellar lengths.

claims.claim: Departure of kinesin from the tip is independent of flagellar length and departure of retrograde trains.
claims.source: The tip resting time of KAP remained nearly constant at different steady-state flagellar lengths (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and was shorter than that of IFT27, indicating that departure of kinesin from the tip is independent of flagellar length and departure of retrograde trains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the constant tip resting time of KAP across different flagellar lengths.

claims.claim: The majority (89%, N = 95) of KAP-GFPs simultaneously departed from the tip in a single step.
claims.source: Unlike IFT trains, the majority (89%, N = 95) of KAP-GFPs simultaneously departed from the tip in a single step (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the PhotoGate experiments.

claims.claim: Each anterograde train contains multiple (6) KAP-GFPs on average.
claims.source: Because each anterograde train contains multiple (6) KAP-GFPs on average (Engel et al., 2009), this observation indicates that kinesin-II departs from the tip in the same oligomeric state as it arrives.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claims.claim: Kinesin-II departs from the tip in the same oligomeric state as it arrives.
claims.source: Because each anterograde train contains multiple (6) KAP-GFPs on average (Engel et al., 2009), this observation indicates that kinesin-II departs from the tip in the same oligomeric state as it arrives.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that KAP-GFPs depart simultaneously despite multiple copies per train.

claims.claim: After KAP detaches from the flagellar tip, it freely explores the space between the flagellar membrane and the axonemal surface rather than sliding along microtubules.
claims.source: We concluded that after KAP detaches from the flagellar tip, it freely explores the space between the flagellar membrane and the axonemal surface rather than sliding along microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lateral fluctuation measurements during diffusion.

claims.claim: Both tagged motors were expressed at near wild-type levels in the d1blic::D1bLIC-crCherry KAP-GFP strain.
claims.source: Both tagged motors were expressed at near wild-type levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from Western blot analysis.

claims.claim: Strong co-localization of D1bLIC-crCherry and KAP-GFP on anterograde trajectories was observed.
claims.source: We observed strong co-localization of D1bLIC-crCherry and KAP-GFP on anterograde trajectories (Figure 4a), demonstrating that dynein-1b is carried to the flagellar tip by kinesin-II.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the two-color imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Dynein-1b is carried to the flagellar tip by kinesin-II.
claims.source: We observed strong co-localization of D1bLIC-crCherry and KAP-GFP on anterograde trajectories (Figure 4a), demonstrating that dynein-1b is carried to the flagellar tip by kinesin-II.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-localization observed in the two-color imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Only D1bLIC-crCherry trains showed robust retrograde transport, while retrograde traces of KAP-GFP were rarely observed.
claims.source: Only D1bLIC-crCherry trains showed robust retrograde transport, while retrograde traces of KAP-GFP were rarely observed, consistent with dissociation of kinesin-II from IFT trains at the tip.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the two-color imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Kinesin-II and dynein-1b exit the flagellar tip independently from each other.
claims.source: These results suggest that kinesin-II and dynein-1b exit the flagellar tip independently from each other.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the two-color PhotoGate experiments showing variable order of departure.

claims.claim: The diffusion constant calculated from the fluorescence recovery (1.8 ± 0.1 μm2 s−1) was similar to the result of the MSD analysis.
claims.source: The diffusion constant calculated from the fluorescence recovery (1.8 ± 0.1 μm2 s−1, Figure 5b) was similar to the result of the MSD analysis (Figure 3h).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of two independent measurements from different experimental approaches.

claims.claim: The fluorescent background in KAP-GFP flagella increased towards the tip, suggesting a net efflux of diffusing KAP-GFP towards the cell body.
claims.source: The fluorescent background in KAP-GFP flagella increased towards the tip, suggesting a net efflux of diffusing KAP-GFP towards the cell body (Figure 5c,d).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the imaging experiments and an inference about the direction of net flux.

claims.claim: During flagellar regrowth, the KAP-GFP gradient was maintained for all flagellar lengths.
claims.source: During flagellar regrowth, the KAP-GFP gradient was maintained for all flagellar lengths (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the flagellar regrowth experiments.

claims.claim: The influx of KAP-GFP fluorescence to the flagellum through anterograde IFT was statistically indistinguishable from the efflux of KAP-GFP to the base through one-dimensional diffusion in flagella.
claims.source: The influx of KAP-GFP fluorescence to the flagellum through anterograde IFT was statistically indistinguishable from the efflux of KAP-GFP to the base through one-dimensional diffusion in flagella (Welch's t-test, p=0.80, N = 57, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of influx and efflux measurements with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: KAP-GFP returns to the cell body by diffusing from the flagellar tip.
claims.source: These results strongly indicate that KAP-GFP returns to the cell body by diffusing from the flagellar tip.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRAP experiments and flux measurements.

claims.claim: The total amount of KAP localized to the base and flagellum increased by two-fold with flagellar length.
claims.source: The total amount of KAP localized to the base and flagellum increased by two-fold with flagellar length, indicating the upregulation of IFT components during flagellar growth.
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the confocal microscopy experiments during flagellar regrowth.

claims.claim: IFT components are upregulated during flagellar growth.
claims.source: The total amount of KAP localized to the base and flagellum increased by two-fold with flagellar length, indicating the upregulation of IFT components during flagellar growth.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the increase in total KAP fluorescence during flagellar regrowth.

claims.claim: The fluorescence intensity at the flagellar base was highest for short flagella (1–4 µm) and decreased ~4 fold as cells grew full-length flagella (~10 µm).
claims.source: The fluorescence intensity at the flagellar base was highest for short flagella (1–4 µm) and decreased ~4 fold as cells grew full-length flagella (~10 µm, Figure 6b), significantly larger than ~1.6 fold reduction reported previously (Ludington et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the confocal microscopy experiments during flagellar regrowth.

claims.claim: The KAP fluorescence in the flagellum was low in short flagella and increased ~10 fold as the flagellar length reached the steady-state.
claims.source: We also observed that the KAP fluorescence in the flagellum was low in short flagella and increased ~10 fold as the flagellar length reached the steady-state (Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement from the confocal microscopy experiments during flagellar regrowth.

claims.claim: Unlike KAP-GFP, basal body fluorescence of IFT20-GFP remained nearly constant across all flagellar lengths.
claims.source: Unlike KAP-GFP, basal body fluorescence of IFT20-GFP remained nearly constant across all flagellar lengths in IFT20::IFT20-GFP cells (Figure 6c), presumably because they are rapidly returned to the base through active transport.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the confocal microscopy experiments during flagellar regrowth.

claims.claim: IFT20-GFP is rapidly returned to the base through active transport.
claims.source: Unlike KAP-GFP, basal body fluorescence of IFT20-GFP remained nearly constant across all flagellar lengths in IFT20::IFT20-GFP cells (Figure 6c), presumably because they are rapidly returned to the base through active transport.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the constant basal body fluorescence of IFT20-GFP.

claims.claim: Chlamydomonas grows ~1.5X longer flagella in the presence of Li+.
claims.source: Chlamydomonas grows ~1.5X longer flagella in the presence of Li+ (Nakamura et al., 1987) by recruiting flagellar proteins from the cell body pool into the flagella (Nakamura et al., 1987) rather than requiring new protein synthesis (Wilson and Lefebvre, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: KAP gets depleted at the basal body at equilibrium in Li+ treated cells.
claims.source: In agreement with our model, we observed that KAP gets depleted at the basal body at equilibrium.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the Li+ treatment experiments.

claims.claim: The KAP fluorescence localized to a flagellum correlated strongly with flagellar length (Pearson's R = 0.86) in Li+ treated cells.
claims.source: The KAP fluorescence localized to a flagellum correlated strongly with flagellar length (Pearson's R = 0.86), similar to untreated cells.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the Li+ treatment experimental data.

claims.claim: In the absence of new protein synthesis, Chlamydomonas can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation.
claims.source: In the absence of new protein synthesis, Chlamydomonas can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation, suggesting that the cytoplasmic pool of flagellar proteins is at least one half of that localized to the flagellar compartment (Rosenbaum et al., 1969).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The cytoplasmic pool of flagellar proteins is at least one half of that localized to the flagellar compartment.
claims.source: In the absence of new protein synthesis, Chlamydomonas can grow half-length flagella after deflagellation, suggesting that the cytoplasmic pool of flagellar proteins is at least one half of that localized to the flagellar compartment (Rosenbaum et al., 1969).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that half-length flagella can be grown without new protein synthesis.

claims.claim: Over a wide range of flagellar lengths (2–22 µm), KAP gets depleted at the basal body when the flagella reach their equilibrium length.
claims.source: Therefore, over a wide range of flagellar lengths (2–22 µm), KAP gets depleted at the basal body when the flagella reach their equilibrium length.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiments with control, Li+ treated, and cycloheximide treated cells.

claims.claim: Disassembly of anterograde trains and reassembly of the retrograde trains is a multistep process regulated by extracellular calcium and the concentration of active dynein motors.
claims.source: Kinetic analysis of the tip resting time revealed that disassembly of anterograde trains and reassembly of the retrograde trains is a multistep process regulated by extracellular calcium and the concentration of active dynein motors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Gamma distribution fit and the effects of EGTA and ciliobrevin D treatments.

claims.claim: Kinesin-II drives anterograde trains in a highly processive fashion and then dissociates from the IFT trains when they reach at the flagellar tip.
claims.source: Kinesin-II drives anterograde trains in a highly processive fashion and then dissociates from the IFT trains when they reach at the flagellar tip.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PhotoGate experiments tracking KAP-GFP.

claims.claim: KAP-GFP returns to the flagellar base by diffusing within the flagellum, similar to the diffusion of kinesin-1 in mammalian neurons.
claims.source: KAP-GFP then returns to the flagellar base by diffusing within the flagellum, similar to the diffusion of kinesin-1 in mammalian neurons (Blasius et al., 2013) and in contrast to the retrograde transport of kinesin-II observed in other cilia (Signor et al., 1999; Broekhuis et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2014; Prevo et al., 2015), see below).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FRAP and MSD experiments, with comparison to other systems via citations.

claims.claim: The diffusion of KAP-GFP represents the movement of the entire heterotrimeric kinesin-II complex.
claims.source: We propose that the diffusion of KAP-GFP represents the movement of the entire heterotrimeric kinesin-II complex because KAP and the kinesin-II motor subunits co-sediment in sucrose density gradients of purified flagella extracts (Cole et al., 1998; Mueller et al., 2005) and neither KAP nor FLA10 accumulate in flagella during inactivation of retrograde transport (Engel et al., 2012; Pedersen et al., 2006; Reck et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Dynein-1b is carried as an inactive motor complex on anterograde trains.

claims.claim: Dynein-1b actively engages with microtubules only when it reaches the flagellar tip.

results.result: Anterograde IFT trains split apart at the ciliary tip and IFT complexes from different trains mix with each other to form retrograde trains. PhotoGate experiments showed that 2.4 retrograde trains depart after arrival of a single fluorescent anterograde train, significantly higher than the 1.15 ratio of retrograde to anterograde train frequencies, indicating sub-proportional mixing.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C29-C32 provide converging evidence from PhotoGate experiments showing that anterograde trains split and mix at the tip. The sub-proportional increase in retrograde trains (C30) with increasing numbers of fluorescent anterograde trains (C29) strongly supports the mixing model (C31, C32). Statistical analysis (p=10^-20) and Monte Carlo simulations validate the conclusions.

results.result: IFT train turnaround at the ciliary tip is a rapid multistep process regulated by calcium and dynein activity. The tip resting time of the first retrograde train (3.1±0.3 s) fits a Gamma distribution with shape parameter 3, indicating multiple rate-limiting steps. EGTA treatment increased tip departure time but not remodeling time, while ciliobrevin D increased total tip resting time over two-fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C45 and C82 provide comprehensive kinetic analysis of tip turnaround. The Gamma distribution fit (C34, C35) with appropriate statistical parameters, linear increase in successive train departures (C36, C37), and differential effects of EGTA (C40-C42) and ciliobrevin D (C44, C45) treatments provide strong mechanistic evidence. The y-intercept analysis (C38, C39) distinguishes remodeling from departure processes.

results.result: Dynein-1b is carried to the ciliary tip as inactive cargo on anterograde trains powered by kinesin-II and only becomes active at the tip. Two-color imaging showed strong co-localization of D1bLIC-crCherry and KAP-GFP on anterograde trajectories, with D1bLIC showing similar tip turnaround dynamics to IFT27 (average 2.5 retrograde trains from one anterograde train).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C46, C49-C50, C61-C62, and C86-C87 provide direct evidence from two-color imaging and PhotoGate experiments. The co-localization data (C61, C62) combined with the lack of tug-of-war behavior (C86) and similar tip dynamics to IFT complexes (C49, C50) strongly support the inactive cargo model. The conclusion is further supported by cited literature on inactive dynein states.

results.result: Kinesin-II detaches from IFT trains at the ciliary tip and returns to the basal body by one-dimensional diffusion within the flagellum. KAP-GFP moved anterogradely to the tip (2.0±0.3 μm/s), rested for 2.2±0.2 s, then diffused back with a diffusion constant of 1.68±0.04 μm²/s. The majority (89%) of KAP-GFP departed simultaneously in oligomeric form, and lateral fluctuations during diffusion (65±7 nm) were consistent with free exploration of the flagellar space.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C47-C48, C51-C59, C63-C64, C83-C84 provide comprehensive evidence from PhotoGate, MSD analysis, and lateral fluctuation measurements. The diffusion constant (C53) is consistent with other diffusing proteins in cilia. The simultaneous departure of multiple KAP-GFP molecules (C56) despite their presence in oligomeric form (C57, C58) and the large lateral fluctuations (C59) strongly support free diffusion rather than microtubule-based transport.

results.result: KAP-GFP returns to the cell body by diffusion from the flagellar tip, as demonstrated by FRAP experiments. The diffusion constant from FRAP (1.8±0.1 μm²/s) matched MSD analysis results. A fluorescence gradient increasing toward the tip was maintained during flagellar regrowth, and the influx through anterograde IFT was statistically indistinguishable from efflux by diffusion (p=0.80).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 provide independent validation of the diffusion model through FRAP experiments. The agreement between two independent measurement methods (C65), the maintained gradient during regrowth (C67), and the flux balance analysis (C68) with appropriate statistical testing provide strong support. The conclusion (C69) is well-justified by the converging evidence.

results.result: As flagella elongate, diffusion delays the return of kinesin-II to the basal body, depleting the pool available for anterograde transport. During flagellar regrowth, KAP fluorescence at the basal body decreased ~4-fold while flagellar KAP increased ~10-fold as cells grew full-length flagella. Total KAP increased 2-fold, indicating upregulation during growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C70-C73, C102-C103, C118-C120 provide direct measurements from confocal microscopy during flagellar regrowth. The quantitative changes in KAP distribution (C72, C73) with appropriate sample sizes (N=104 flagella) support the depletion model. The diffusion gradient measurements (C118) and delay calculations (C119, C120) provide mechanistic explanation for the observed depletion.

results.result: Dissociation of kinesin-II from IFT trains serves as a negative feedback mechanism for flagellar length control. KAP depletion at the basal body was observed at equilibrium across a wide range of flagellar lengths (2-22 μm) in control, Li+-treated, and cycloheximide-treated cells. KAP fluorescence in flagella correlated strongly with flagellar length (Pearson's R=0.86).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C77-C78, C81, C104, C110-C111 present the main model of the paper with supporting evidence from multiple experimental conditions. The strong correlation (R=0.86) across different treatments (C78) and the consistent depletion at equilibrium (C81) support the negative feedback model. However, C104 is speculative about consequences, and the model faces challenges from conflicting literature (acknowledged in C121-C123).

results.result: Unlike kinesin-II, IFT components are rapidly recycled by dynein-1b and their abundance at the basal body remains constant during flagellar elongation. IFT20-GFP basal body fluorescence remained nearly constant across all flagellar lengths (N=103 flagella), contrasting with KAP-GFP depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75, C112-C114 provide important control data distinguishing IFT component recycling from kinesin-II recycling. The constant basal body levels of IFT20-GFP (C74, C113) with adequate sample size support the conclusion that IFT components are not limiting (C114), which is further supported by cited literature showing small amounts are sufficient for maintenance.

results.result: IFT trains and motors move at characteristic velocities in Chlamydomonas flagella. IFT27-GFP moved at 2.1±0.4 μm/s anterogradely and 3.0±0.7 μm/s retrogradely (N=80 each direction). D1bLIC and KAP showed similar anterograde velocities.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28, C46-C47 provide basic characterization data with appropriate sample sizes and standard deviations. The velocities are consistent with prior literature and provide validation of the experimental system. These measurements are fundamental to interpreting the PhotoGate experiments.

results.result: The diffusion of KAP-GFP represents movement of the entire heterotrimeric kinesin-II complex based on biochemical evidence. Both tagged motors in the d1blic::D1bLIC-crCherry KAP-GFP strain were expressed at near wild-type levels, and KAP co-sediments with motor subunits in sucrose gradients.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 provides direct evidence from Western blots, but C85 is a proposal based on cited biochemical data rather than direct demonstration in this study. While the co-sedimentation evidence from prior work is supportive, the current study does not directly demonstrate that the entire complex diffuses together. The observation of KAP clusters breaking apart (Video 7) suggests heterogeneity in the diffusing species.

results.result: Prior theoretical and experimental work supports the model that kinesin-II availability limits flagellar growth. A theoretical study showed increased diffusion time can explain the inverse relationship between length and motor recruitment rate, and KAP intensity at the basal body correlates with loading on IFT trains and assembly rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106, C109 cite prior literature that supports the authors' model. These are appropriately presented as supporting evidence from other studies rather than new findings. The citations appear accurate and relevant to the model being proposed.

results.result: The model faces challenges from conflicting literature on kinesin-II levels in mutant strains. Studies show fla10ts and fla3 mutants maintain near full-length flagella despite lower kinesin-II levels, though fla3 shows slower regeneration and more recent work found wild-type kinesin-II levels in fla10ts at permissive temperatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 accurately present challenges to the model from cited literature. The authors appropriately acknowledge these contradictions and provide potential explanations based on the balance-point model (C124). This represents honest assessment of conflicting evidence rather than new experimental findings.

results.result: Background on IFT and ciliary structure establishes the context for the study. IFT is essential for ciliary assembly and maintenance, involves bidirectional transport by kinesin-II and dynein-1b, and trains must be remodeled at turnaround zones, though this cannot be directly observed by conventional microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C26 present established knowledge from the field with appropriate citations. These provide necessary background and motivation for the study. The technical limitation noted in C26 justifies the development of the PhotoGate method. All claims are well-supported by cited literature.

results.result: IFT dynamics in Chlamydomonas differ from other organisms. Chlamydomonas has distinct microtubule track organization with B-tubules terminating before A-tubules, and shows processive movement without frequent pausing, unlike C. elegans or mammalian cilia where kinesin-II is recycled by retrograde transport rather than diffusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C96 compare Chlamydomonas IFT to other systems using appropriate citations. The structural differences (C88-C90) and behavioral differences (C92-C96) are well-documented in cited literature. C91 is appropriately presented as speculation. These comparisons provide important context for understanding why the diffusion mechanism may be specific to Chlamydomonas.

results.result: The balance point model of flagellar length control states that length is set when assembly and disassembly rates reach equilibrium. Assembly rate is determined by IFT train injection, which correlates with material at the basal body, and both train size and cargo loading scale inversely with flagellar length.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 present the established balance point model with appropriate citations. This provides the theoretical framework for interpreting the new findings. The cited literature accurately supports each component of the model.

results.result: Diffusion plays a role in bacterial flagellar length control through a mechanism where flagellins diffuse through the filament channel to reach the assembly site, with longer filaments growing more slowly due to increased diffusion time.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 present an analogy from bacterial systems with appropriate citations. This comparison helps contextualize the eukaryotic findings, though the mechanisms differ (diffusion within a channel vs. diffusion in the flagellar space). The cited literature supports the bacterial mechanism.

results.result: IFT components are upregulated after deflagellation and a large cytoplasmic pool exchanges with the flagellar pool. Cells can grow half-length flagella without new protein synthesis, and IFT is required for efficient removal of axonemal precursors, with flagellar resorption before mitosis occurring faster than disassembly after IFT inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C129 present established knowledge from cited literature about IFT component regulation and turnover. These provide context for understanding the complexity of flagellar length control beyond the kinesin-II depletion mechanism. All claims are appropriately supported by citations.
